<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S6.SS1.SSS0.Px4" title="In 6.1 Comparing SotA LLMs (Table ) ‣ 6 Results ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Majority of models suffer by limited pedagogical instruction following.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S6.SS2" title="In 6 Results ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">6.2 </span>Scaffolding Score - Results</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" title="In 6.2 Scaffolding Score - Results ‣ 6 Results ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Ablation of finetuning data.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" title="In 6.2 Scaffolding Score - Results ‣ 6 Results ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Scores distribution.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-ended
<br class="ltx_break">Pedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluating the pedagogical capabilities of AI-based tutoring models is critical for making guided progress in the field. Yet, we lack a reliable, easy-to-use, and simple-to-run evaluation that reflects the pedagogical abilities of models.
To fill this gap, we present <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span>, an open-source benchmark for holistic tutoring model evaluation. <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> contains a collection of datasets and metrics that broadly cover tutor abilities as defined by learning sciences research in dialog-based teaching. To score the pedagogical quality of open-ended teacher responses, we train a reward model and show it can discriminate expert from novice teacher responses with high accuracy.
We evaluate a wide set of closed- and open-weight models on <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> and find that subject expertise, indicated by solving ability, does not immediately translate to good teaching.
Rather, pedagogy and subject expertise appear to form a trade-off that is navigated by the degree of tutoring specialization of the model.
Furthermore, tutoring appears to become more challenging in longer dialogs, where simpler questioning strategies begin to fail.
We release the benchmark, code, and leaderboard openly
to enable rapid benchmarking of future models.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para"><img src="2502.18940v1/figures/github.png" id="p2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:13/13;" width="13" height="13" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.2pt;"><a href="https://github.com/eth-lre/mathtutorbench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">github.com/eth-lre/mathtutorbench</a></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) present an opportunity to transform education by offering ubiquitous access to individualized tutoring <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jurenka et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.18940v1/skills_new2.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:357/353;" width="357" height="353" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
Effective teaching requires various skills which we categorize into expertise, student understanding, and pedagogical ability. <span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> evalutes these according to the tasks shown in the outer ring.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While these models excel at generating correct answers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al. (2023)</a></cite>, experienced teachers
help students think for themselves and do not just give away answers to make learning effortless <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
Teaching involves a combination of skills including subject expertise, the ability to diagnose and correct student mistakes, and the application of sound pedagogical techniques. For example, teachers need to know when to withhold answers from students, use Socratic questioning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anghileri (2006)</a></cite>, or how to engage them cognitively in problem solving <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi and Wylie (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapur (2016)</a></cite>.
Therefore, a crucial element of building LLM tutors is their evaluation; it is critical to understand whether their guidance is helpful to prevent harm, and to guide progress in future model development.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Yet, current evaluation practices do not meet these criteria.
On the one hand, automatic metrics usually evaluate tutoring models by measuring the word overlap between a ground-truth response and a generated response <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tack et al. (2023)</a></cite>, or focus exclusively on question-answering performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chevalier et al. (2024)</a></cite>. This is fast but arguably fails to capture the intricacies of tutoring.
Although human evaluation might be a way to capture these nuances by defining suitable criteria to capture them <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tack and Piech, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maurya et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, it is expensive. Importantly, it can only create a snapshot of current performance and cannot be used to evaluate or compare to future models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we fill this gap by releasing <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span>, a collection of datasets and metrics to holistically evaluate dialog tutoring models for math tutoring. Teaching is a complex and multifaceted task that extends beyond subject mastery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nye et al. (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tack et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite>.
Therefore, <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> is divided into three categories: <em id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">math expertise</em> which evaluates the subject-matter expertise of the tutor, <em id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">student understanding</em> which evaluates the tutor’s ability to verify, locate and correct student solutions, and <em id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">teacher response generation</em> which evaluates the scaffolding abilities of the tutor.
Math expertise and student understanding are evaluated based on standard metrics, and we propose a novel metric for evaluating teacher response generation.
In particular, we train a small and quick-to-run reward model by contrasting effective and less effective tutor utterances in terms of structured scaffolding guidance with questions and hints instead of giving away the answer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anghileri, 2006</a>)</cite>.
The reward model is then used to score tutor model generations.
We show that this metric is reliable by showing that it can distinguish utterances from expert teachers from those stemming from novice teachers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> with high accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate various open- and closed-weight state-of-the-art LLMs and specialized tutoring models on <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span>.
Our results show that there is a trade-off between subject expertise and pedagogical abilities that is dependent on the degree of specialization of a tutoring LLM.
Specializing an LLM for pedagogy comes at the cost of solving ability and, conversely, a high solving accuracy often means that the LLM lacks pedagogy.
Still, more specialized tutoring models tend to retain their teaching abilities even further into a dialog with a student, while general models quickly become worse.
With this, our work contributes to accelerating the development of tutoring LLMs by providing a holistic benchmark that can be evaluated quickly and fairly using automatic metrics.
We release our code and data publicly to promote open research on tutoring LLMs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S1.F2.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:scale(22383945,22383945) ;"><img src="2502.18940v1/figure1_v4.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:496/266;" width="496" height="266" alt="Refer to caption">
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Overview of the <span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">MathTutorBench</span> benchmark. Each benchmark task defines a dataset, system prompts with problem and dialog, metric, and ground-truth teacher responses. A reward model is used to score the pedagogical quality over teacher responses (win rate). The right part of the figure shows the outcome as a performance comparison of selected LLMs. While they all perform well in a simple problem-solving setting, most of them lack in correct detection of mistakes and generating pedagogical responses.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>LLM-Based Dialog Tutoring</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A good tutor should scaffold student learning in a structured way rather than just provide correct answers.
Current approaches to dialog tutoring using LLMs try to achieve this by differnent means: prompt-based elicitation of pedagogical behavior, finetuning models on pedagogical conversations, and alignment with pedagogical preferences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, most existing works use LLMs with a carefully chosen prompt which enumerates desired pedagogical behavior. Bridge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite> analyzes the teacher behavior and proposes to structure the prompt into a sequence of decisions, similar to real teachers, first to infer the error type and then to determine the pedagogical intent. Other works mostly directly write extensive prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sonkar et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kargupta et al. (2024)</a></cite>. However, defining such prompts is tedious, sensitive to small changes and difficult to test <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jurenka et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Second, several approaches finetune models on real or mostly synthetically generated data.
SocraticLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024)</a></cite> uses a GPT-4 judge to evaluate the quality of teacher guidance using correctness and Socratic principles. A similar approach is to role-model teacher and student conversations based on textbook data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chevalier et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024a)</a></cite>. MathDial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Macina et al. (2023a)</a></cite> is one of the few works that use teachers’ utterances when interacting with students to finetune models. However, it is expensive to collect such data on a larger scale. Therefore, LearnLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2024)</a></cite>
uses an empirically validated mixture of synthetic and teacher-created datasets. However, for capturing high-quality tutoring, teacher-created data is essential and therefore upweighted in their final data mix.
Finally, LLMs can be aligned for pedagogical preferences during post-training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2024)</a></cite>, because these are usually tacit. However, no datasets are openly available or they rely on larger models such as GPT-4 as a judge which limits its generalizability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our benchmark contributes an important missing ingredient in the development of LLM-based tutors – the ability to quickly evaluate and compare models on key pedagogical aspects.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Automatic &amp; Human Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several works rely on automatic NLG metrics such as BLEU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papineni et al. (2002)</a></cite> or BERTScore <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2020)</a></cite> for evaluation which require human-annotated ground truths. However, since tutoring has the goal of helping students learn  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Macina et al. (2023b)</a></cite>, it is very open-ended and there is no single best pedagogical approach at each turn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jurenka et al. (2024)</a></cite>. This results in noisy and unreliable scores from automatic metrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tack et al. (2023)</a></cite>. There exists an educational-specific classifier of active teacher listening <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Demszky et al. (2021)</a></cite>, however, it is limited to only this one dimension of teaching and does not account for the entire dialog history.
Therefore, recent finetuned tutoring LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chevalier et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024)</a></cite> rely on GPT-4-as-a-judge on dimensions like helpfulness and presentation. Some works on reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al. (2024)</a></cite> also focus on multi-turn model abilities judged by GPT-4 but they lack an educational focus.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Pedagogical quality annotation requires hiring teachers, but it is time-consuming and hard to compare across trials. Two papers recently addressed the issue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tack and Piech (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maurya et al. (2024)</a></cite> by providing evaluation taxonomies but only present one-off static snapshots of current models’ performance without the possibility to automatically evaluate new models.
Finally, measuring student learning gains directly focuses on the end goal. However, learner studies are costly, time-consuming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmucker et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and with strict ethics and privacy requirements. There is a growing interest in designing proper evaluation guidelines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tack et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jurenka et al. (2024)</a></cite>, however, there is still a need for a unified automatic evaluation for scalable model development.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> addresses the limitations of existing automatic metrics by focusing specifically on tutoring, is simple to run, replicable, and could serve as a proxy for deciding which models to focus on in human studies. Moreover, our benchmark only uses data collected from real teachers.</p>
</div>

<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Background</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Next Teacher Utterance Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on educational dialogues between a student and a teacher, where a student is trying to solve a multi-step problem <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{p}$}$}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐩</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{p}$}$}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The problem has a single numerical solution <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐚</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}</annotation></semantics></math></span> and a sequence of solution steps <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}=(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{1},\dots,\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{N})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}=(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{1},\dots,\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{N})}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{n}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{n}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{N}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\smash{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{N}}</annotation></semantics></math> contains the final answer
<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐚</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}</annotation></semantics></math></span>.
A student solution consists of steps <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\smash{\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}=(\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}_{1},\dots,\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}_{M})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\smash{\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}=(\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}_{1},\dots,\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}_{M})}</annotation></semantics></math> and the first step with a mistake is <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e\in\{0,1,\dots,M\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e\in\{0,1,\dots,M\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e=0</annotation></semantics></math> means no mistake.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The goal of dialog tutoring is to continue an existing teacher-student dialog <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}\coloneqq(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{1},\dots,\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}\coloneqq(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{1},\dots,\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T-1})</annotation></semantics></math> consisting of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T-1</annotation></semantics></math> turns <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{t}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{t}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> with a new turn <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}\in\mathcal{V}^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> that simulates the teacher and guides the student towards solving a problem.
This is usually done by learning a model
<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{\mbox{$\mbox{$\boldsymbol{\theta}$}$}}}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}\mid\mathcal{H},\mathcal{K},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐢</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{\mbox{$\mbox{$\boldsymbol{\theta}$}$}}}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}\mid\mathcal{H},\mathcal{K},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> with parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\boldsymbol{\theta}$}$}\in\real^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝜽</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\boldsymbol{\theta}$}$}\in\real^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is optionally conditioned on background knowledge <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}</annotation></semantics></math> (in our case only the problem <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}</annotation></semantics></math></span>) and a teacher intent <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐢</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, and using a decoding strategy, such as greedy decoding or sampling according to <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{\mbox{$\mbox{$\boldsymbol{\theta}$}$}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝜽</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{\mbox{$\mbox{$\boldsymbol{\theta}$}$}}}</annotation></semantics></math> to generate an output.
The turn <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> should then fulfill the desiderate laid out in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Learning Sciences Principles ‣ 3 Background ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.
The goal of this work is to present a benchmark to understand the quality of various <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> generated by different models <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S3.SS1.p2.m13.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math></span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Learning Sciences Principles</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on 1:1 multi-turn teacher-student interactions where teachers promote active learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Freeman et al. (2014)</a></cite> by engaging students through scaffolding nudges, hints, and Socratic questioning. Based on effective teaching research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lepper and Woolverton (2002)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi and Wylie (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nye et al. (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jurenka et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we define the following pedagogical principles: <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(a) correctness:</span> the teacher should guide the student towards the correct answer and not state incorrect facts; <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(b) scaffolding instead of giving away the answer:</span> the teacher should help the student to cognitively engage with the problem and discover the answer on their own; <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(c) encourage self-correction:</span> by correctly identifying the student mistake and first giving the student the opportunity to self-correct and learn from a mistake; <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(d) not overload student:</span> manage cognitive load by not giving too much information at once.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>MathTutorBench</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span>, a benchmark that evaluates the tutoring capabilities of tutoring models. <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> consists of three high-level skills that a good human teacher needs to have <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bommasani et al. (2021)</a></cite>: <span id="S4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Expertise</span>, <span id="S4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Student Understanding</span> and <span id="S4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Pedagogical Abilities</span>. These skills are tested by seven different tasks, each consisting of a dataset, prompt, and metric. All tasks in <span id="S4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> are related to math tutoring. The problems are mostly sourced from GSM8k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al. (2021)</a></cite>.
Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Automatic &amp; Human Evaluation ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the datasets and tasks. The prompts used for the tasks in the benchmark are shown in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Task Prompts ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<div id="S4.T2.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:78.4pt;vertical-align:-37.9pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-149.7pt,34.0pt) scale(0.535436324365584,0.535436324365584) ;">

<td id="S4.T2.2.1.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">0.90</td>
<td id="S4.T2.2.1.8.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_rr"><span id="S4.T2.2.1.8.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.48</span></td>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>We find that expertise and student understanding form a trade-off with pedagogy in tutor response generation. Models are grouped into general, specialized tutoring, and math reasoning models. The win rate is computed as the rate of the reward model preferring model responses over teacher responses. IF = Instruction Following.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Tasks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section explains each task and complements Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Automatic &amp; Human Evaluation ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> with the rationale for including it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1. Problem Solving.</span> We include a math word problem solving task that measures the accuracy of the final numeric answer generated with chain-of-thought <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2022)</a></cite> compared to the answer <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐚</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}</annotation></semantics></math></span>. Even though this type of evaluation is popular, saturated, and contaminated, in <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> it serves as an indicator of a balance between expertise and pedagogical abilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2. Socratic Questioning.</span> Socratic questioning is related to the problem decomposition to smaller and more manageable parts.
This task is to evaluate whether a model generates for each correct step <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> at least one corresponding guidance question <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{q}$}$}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐪</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{q}$}$}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> towards the correct answer, which could be posed to the student instead of simply providing the answer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shridhar et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3. Student Solution Correctness.</span>
This task evaluates a teacher’s ability to verify the correctness of a student’s answer. Framed as a balanced binary classification
task based on student solution chain <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{s}</annotation></semantics></math>, this dimension ensures that the model can objectively discern whether a student’s reply is correct or incorrect, a crucial prerequisite for providing accurate feedback and identification of misconceptions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4. Student Mistake Location.</span>
Mistake location is a critical component of effective tutoring, focusing on a teacher’s ability to accurately identify the exact location of the first mistake in a student’s response <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐬</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{s}$}$}}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Daheim et al. (2024)</a></cite>. This task assesses whether a tutoring model can pinpoint where a student’s reasoning has gone wrong, enabling timely and precise feedback. By detecting steps with mistakes, the model can help students understand their misconceptions and steer the conversation to mitigate them, thus fostering a more productive learning experience <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapur (2016)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5. Student Mistake Correction.</span>
This task measures the performance of a model to generate a reasoning chain with a correct final numeric answer <span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S4.SS1.p6.m1.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐚</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}</annotation></semantics></math></span> even though the student proposes an incorrect answer in the dialog history <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>. The conditioning on dialog history is the difference to Problem Solving. We test the models’ ability to handle incorrect solutions. Models should not get derailed by students’ incorrect steps. From a broader perspective, even if there is an incorrect step in a dialog history <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>, this tests the recovery of a model from mistakes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6. Scaffolding Generation (scaff.).</span>
The task is to generate the next teacher utterance <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐮</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{u}$}$}_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> as a continuation of the dialog. As it is an open-ended task, we use a reward model to score generations over teacher responses (explained in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Scaffolding Score ‣ 4 MathTutorBench ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) to estimate its’ pedagogical quality.
The tasks consist of two variations. <span id="S4.SS1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Scaffolding generation</span> focuses on generating an immediate response to a student’s incorrect solution.
We use a simple prompt for this version asking models to respond to a student as “an experienced math teacher in a useful and caring way“ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite>. The second version is <span id="S4.SS1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">scaffolding generation [hard]</span>, a variant with a longer conversation history (avg. 5.78 turns).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">7. Pedagogical Instruction Following (IF) for Scaffolding Generation.</span> The task refers to the ability of the model to follow pedagogical instructions in prompts and steer the model generations to be more desired <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2024)</a></cite>. In this task, we use the LearnLM ‘extended‘ prompt <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jurenka et al. (2024)</a></cite> which specifically enumerates desired behaviors
such as “nudging students”, “asking guiding questions”, and “not overwhelm student”.
Therefore, in contrast to a simple prompt from <span id="S4.SS1.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">scaffolding generation</span>, we hypothesize that models should improve their generations to be more aligned with our set of guiding principles from Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Background ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. The same is applied to the hard portion of the dataset.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Datasets</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The requirements for the dataset included in the benchmark are to focus on middle school math content and contain 1:1 tutoring conversations written by human teachers. We found two datasets that fit the criteria, Bridge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite> and MathDial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Macina et al. (2023a)</a></cite>. We excluded NCTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Demszky and Hill (2023)</a></cite> dataset because it is multi-persona.
Bridge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite> contains 700 snippets of real online tutoring conversations by novice teachers, where each response is revised by an expert teacher. MathDial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Macina et al. (2023a)</a></cite> consists of 2.9k tutoring conversations collected by human teachers who interacted with simulated students. Both datasets focus on math, Bridge uses various problem sources and MathDial sources problems from GSM8k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al. (2021)</a></cite>; a dataset of math word problems that we used in the expertise task. We combine Bridge and MathDial datasets into a combined dataset called <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">MathDialBridge</span> which we further split into one with a maximum of 4 utterances and the rest we put into <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">MathDialBridge[hard]</span>.
Finally, we use the StepVerify <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Daheim et al. (2024)</a></cite> dataset which builds on top of the MathDial student incorrect solutions and introduces annotation of the first erroneous step in a student solution. Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Automatic &amp; Human Evaluation ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> describes all the datasets and their statistics.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Scaffolding Score</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluating pedagogical abilities in tutoring is inherently challenging due to the open-ended nature of the involved tasks. Unlike more structured domains like factual question answering, pedagogy requires assessing the quality of responses such as questioning guidance to the root cause of a mistake, and actionability of productive scaffolding. In other words, we need an efficient and lightweight mechanism, a critic model, that can assign a meaningful score to a generative model’s output based on its pedagogical effectiveness.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.1 </span>Criteria-based Scoring</h4>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.18940v1/model_reward_scores_comparison.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/333;" width="476" height="333"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Models performance on pairwise judgment of teacher responses. We compute accuracy on an independent test set
based on Bridge dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite>
as a proportion of Expert teacher responses preferred over Novice teacher responses.
Extended prompt enumerates our pedagogical criteria (Figure  <a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ C.2 Implementation details ‣ Appendix C Reward Model Details ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The most straightforward approach is to train individual critic models for each pedagogical task using labeled data.
For an evaluation taxonomy with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> total evaluation criteria,
for each criterion <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> we train a binary classifier <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})</annotation></semantics></math> that outputs a binary prediction of whether the criteria is present or not in response <span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m4.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}</annotation></semantics></math></span>. To combine these into a final score for a response, we aggregate them as <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i=1}^{n}C_{i}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{n}C_{i}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})</annotation></semantics></math>, which represents a discrete score of the total number of predicted desired criteria for the response.
For example, MRBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maurya et al. (2024)</a></cite> is a small dataset annotated with 8 criteria such as the presence of guidance, actionability, and telling the answer.
However, the scale of the required data and sparse features pose significant challenges.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.2 </span>Pairwise Ranking of Teacher Responses</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since labeled data for each criterion can be scarce, we here explore a more unified strategy. Instead of training a separate model for each criterion, where each annotation criterion has inherent subjectivity, we relax the objective and train a single critic model that aggregates multiple criteria into a pairwise comparison.
We train a reward model using binary ranking loss by following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al. (2022)</a></cite>:</p>
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}=-\log\sigma\left(r_{\theta}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{x}$}$},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{c})-r_{\theta}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{x}$}$},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{r})-m\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>rank</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}=-\log\sigma\left(r_{\theta}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{x}$}$},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{c})-r_{\theta}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{x}$}$},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{r})-m\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\theta}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{x}$}$},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\theta}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{x}$}$},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})</annotation></semantics></math> is the scalar score for prompt <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m2.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math></span> and generation <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m3.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}</annotation></semantics></math></span>, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> are preferred (chosen) and rejected generations respectively. The margin <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{c},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{c},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{r})</annotation></semantics></math> represents the numerical quality difference between the chosen and rejected response but may also be set to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.3 </span>Pairwise Preference Data Pipeline</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To create pairwise preference data, we follow our pedagogical criteria from Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Learning Sciences Principles ‣ 3 Background ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. For example, a response is preferred if it is a Socratic question <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{q}$}$}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐪</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{q}$}$}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> or it has dialog intent <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐢</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> which probes student understanding.
Contrary, a response is chosen as dispreferred if it contains part(s) of the reference solution <span id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m3.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}</annotation></semantics></math></span> or has a lower number of desired criteria.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To formalize this, for a given dialog history <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> and a taxonomy with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> criteria, we define a score for each response <span id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath"><math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m3.m1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}</annotation></semantics></math></span>:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbbm{1}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}\text{ has desired criterion }i)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mn>𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mtext> has desired criterion </mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbbm{1}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}\text{ has desired criterion }i)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbbm{1}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbbm{1}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the indicator function that equals 1 if <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cdot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋅</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cdot</annotation></semantics></math> holds and 0 otherwise.
The condition within the indicator function is determined by: a) human criteria annotations (for MRBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maurya et al. (2024)</a></cite>), b) dialog intent annotations <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐢</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{i}$}$}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> of the used pedagogical strategy (for MathDial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Macina et al. (2023a)</a></cite>), and c) subquestion annotation <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{q}$}$}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐪</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{q}$}$}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (for GSM8k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al. (2021)</a></cite>). For each pair of responses <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct a dataset of preference-label pairs <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\{(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})\mid f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i})&gt;f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\{(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})\mid f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i})&gt;f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the margin is defined as <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})=f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i})-f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i},\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})=f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{i})-f(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math>. The dataset captures the relative preference between responses based on the number of desired criteria they exhibit. The description of the datasets used for training and testing is found in Table <a href="#A0.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Ablation of <span id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct</span> reward model. Total number of training instances in brackets. + indicates an addition to the model. Pretraining uses 20% of Ultrafeedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cui et al. (2024)</a></cite>. We select the most accurate model to calculate the Scaffolding score. </figcaption>
</figure>
