</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Models</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">MathTutorBench</span> includes an evaluation of three groups of models: general LLMs, LLM tutors, and math reasoners.
General LLMs such as open-weight <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Llama3.1</span> 70B and 8B, newer <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Llama3.2</span> 3B model, and closed source <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span>. We use specialized tutoring models, namely closed-sourced <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LearnLM-1.5-Pro</span> and recent open-source tutoring models <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-7B-SocraticLM</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024)</a></cite> and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Llemma-7B-32K-MathMix (ScienceTutor)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chevalier et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
To measure the importance of specially finetuned tutoring models, we evaluate the <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct</span>, which is optimized for math reasoning and was used for finetuning the specialized tutor model SocraticLM.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Scaffolding Score - Test Set and Metrics</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The goal of the Scaffolding score is to estimate the pedagogical quality of the teacher response generation.
To validate it, we build a test set containing 482 examples based on Bridge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite> which contains student dialogs with novice teachers. The test set has no instance or problem overlap with our training data. In Bridge, novice teacher responses are improved by expert teachers following an expert-defined decision-making process. The process first identifies the type of the error and then determines the pedagogical strategy and intent. For example, while novice teachers tend to explicitly correct student mistakes by giving away correct answers to students, expert teachers use various scaffolding nudges such as the Socratic method, use hints, or ask for further elaboration of the problematic part.
We use the following formula to compute the accuracy of pairwise ranking between expert teacher and novice teacher:</p>
<table id="S5.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbbm{1}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{\text{expert},i}&gt;\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{\text{novice},i})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mn>𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mrow><mtext>expert</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_markedasmath">𝐲</mi><mrow><mtext>novice</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbbm{1}(\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{\text{expert},i}&gt;\mbox{$\mbox{$\mathbf{y}$}$}_{\text{novice},i}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Scaffolding Score - Models and Baselines</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use LLM-as-a-judge prompting as a baseline, similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jurenka et al. (2024)</a></cite>. For this, we use <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct</span>, <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GPT-4o-mini</span>, and the specialized judge model <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Prompetheus-7b-v2.0</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Moreover, we pick well-performing existing preference-tuned reward models with high scores from the RewardBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lambert et al. (2024)</a></cite> on a variety of chat comparisons, namely, <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Internlm2-7b-reward</span> and <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B-v0.2</span>.
To finetune single criteria-based binary classifiers we use <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ModernBERT<math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Warner et al., 2024</a>)</cite> with a classification head. Finally, we use <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct</span> and <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct</span> for finetuning on preference data, which are small enough to run fast as a part of the benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we showcase our core findings on <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span> and demonstrate the robustness and quality of the scaffolding reward model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Comparing SotA LLMs (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4 MathTutorBench ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>)</h3>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Math expertise does not translate directly to student understanding and pedagogy.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluations reveal a striking imbalance in current language models. While these models exhibit impressive domain knowledge and excel at Problem solving, as evidenced by their performance on datasets like GSM8K, they consistently fall short in Scaffolding generation task. This is particularly clear for Qwen2.5-Math and GPT4o.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Specialized tutoring models improve in pedagogy but do not retain the full solving abilities.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The specialized tutoring model SocraticLM achieves good Scaffolding scores for its size and big improvements over the base model (Qwen2.5-Math). However, it degrades in all Student
Understanding tasks. Compared to SocraticLM, the ScienceTutor degrades in math expertise but has significantly better Student correctness solution and pedagogical instruction following. Closed-sourced LearnLM achieves a more reasonable balance across all skills and tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tutoring is more challenging on longer dialogs.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As indicated by the drop in performance in the win rate of tasks, indicated with ‘hard‘, the longer the context it is more difficult for more to adapt. For example, it might be important to guide students differently than with a simple Socratic questioning. Only LearnLM can keep consistent performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Majority of models suffer by limited pedagogical instruction following.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When we compare scaffolding generation with instruction following win rate (in base and hard splits), we notice that GPT4o follows the pedagogical instructions and gains a significant improvement (similarly, there is a smaller improvement for ScienceTutor). However, other models such as the SocraticLM, LearnLM, or Llama models show decreased or similar performance
suggesting a limited ability to follow pedagogical instructions defined in prompt.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Scaffolding Score - Results</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3.1 Criteria-based Scoring ‣ 4.3 Scaffolding Score ‣ 4 MathTutorBench ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows a comparison between various models evaluated on the task of scoring expert teacher responses higher than novice teacher responses, see Equation <a href="#S5.E3" title="In 5.2 Scaffolding Score - Test Set and Metrics ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
LLM-as-a-judge models are sensitive to prompts and positional bias, so we randomize the order. We report simple and extended prompts with detailing pedagogical guidelines (Figure <a href="#A3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ C.2 Implementation details ‣ Appendix C Reward Model Details ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and <a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ C.2 Implementation details ‣ Appendix C Reward Model Details ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) but their accuracy is lower than 0.7.
Performance of reward models from RewardBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lambert et al. (2024)</a></cite> on the pedagogical preferences is only slightly higher than random.
We also train a combination of criteria-based ModernBERT binary classifiers aggregated into a summed final score, however, it lags behind extended-prompted LLM-as-a-judge models (for individual criterion performance see Table <a href="#A4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix D Details on Single-Criteria Classifiers ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). We hypothesize the single criterion data are highly sparse, noisy and imbalanced, and do not have sufficient data size to work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To summarize, Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3.1 Criteria-based Scoring ‣ 4.3 Scaffolding Score ‣ 4 MathTutorBench ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that finetuning reward models on pedagogical preference data is essential, as these finetuned reward models outperform both LLMs-as-a-judge models and SoTA reward models from RewardBench, consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al. (2024)</a></cite>. We hypothesize that this is because of the lack of pedagogical datasets and a fundamental shift between a better chat response and a better pedagogical response.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation of finetuning data.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.3.3 Pairwise Preference Data Pipeline ‣ 4.3 Scaffolding Score ‣ 4 MathTutorBench ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the results for various data mixtures of pedagogical preference data. We see that synthetic inpainted data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al. (2022)</a></cite> using stepwise questions and answers from GSM8k do not lead to a significant improvement over the base model. However, using pedagogical preference pairs based on human annotators scores <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maurya et al. (2024)</a></cite> improves the score to <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8</annotation></semantics></math>, more than any other baseline in Table <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3.1 Criteria-based Scoring ‣ 4.3 Scaffolding Score ‣ 4 MathTutorBench ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. However, as this dataset contains mostly model generations, only one of the responses is from a human teacher, and they are highly underrepresented. Therefore, we also include conversations from the MathDial training set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Macina et al. (2023a)</a></cite>, which is filtered by desired dialog acts (more details in Table <a href="#A0.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). The resulting finetuned model achieves the best accuracy of 0.84. As the test set is completely separate and no problems are shared between the train and test set, we pick this reward model as our final model for computing the Scaffolding score for model generation win rates over teacher responses (proportion of model generations preferred over teacher responses).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scores distribution.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Additionaly, we plot in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3.3 Pairwise Preference Data Pipeline ‣ 4.3 Scaffolding Score ‣ 4 MathTutorBench ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> the model distribution over scores on the test set. The prompted model with extended prompt and the vanilla model cannot separate the teacher and novice responses as well as the finetuned model. This supports the idea that pedagogical criteria are unique compared to general preference data and we need high-quality pedagogical preference data.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work we propose <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MathTutorBench</span>, a holistic benchmark for quick and cost-effective assessment of the educational capabilities of LLM tutoring models.
It fills a crucial gap in the literature, as it allows fast prototyping of models
by using only lightweight automatic and learned metrics to evaluate pedagogy.
The goal is to not replace human studies measuring learning outcomes, but rather to serve as a measure of which models to use and compare. Finally, we benchmark various
models and report a trade-off between expertise, understanding, and pedagogy, as well as diminishing results on longer tutoring conversations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work focuses on high school math tutoring and limits the insights of the benchmark to multi-step math problems. Despite a limited number of available conversation dataset in other domains, we plan to extend the benchmark to further STEM domains to generalize its applicability and reach.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The conversational data in the benchmark does not contain conversations longer than 10 turns and thus can miss to evaluate very long educational conversations with long-term dependencies which might be present in online tutoring classes.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We study 1:1 conversational tutoring between teacher and student in this work. Specifically, we focus on a teacher using hints and nudges to aid student learning and provide engaging learning opportunities for students. However, there are additional functions of a teacher that we decided not to model, for example building rapport or trust with less engaged students.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark does not contain all possible dimensions for educational evaluation. For example, it is missing a safety evaluation of potentially harmful tutor responses. It is an extensive research area and not the goal of this work. However, as the benchmark is open-source we plan to extend it to include more safety evaluations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Ethics Statement</h2>

<section id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Intended usage</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The goal of the benchmark is to evaluate new and existing dialog tutoring models on the skills related to math expertise, student understanding, and pedagogical capabilities. We will release the code and the dataset under CC-BY-4.0 license. This follows the licences of all the datasets which we are using in the benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Accessibility and Potential Misuse</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The main goal of our work is to encourage the community to use the benchmark to improve existing tutoring models by balancing expertise, student understanding, and proper pedagogical guidance. However, there are potential risks related to the data and the scoring reward model. Models could optimize for reward hacking which could lead to suboptimal tutoring behaviour. Moreover, if the data contains some unknown pattern, the risk is that this could be exploited by new models to achieve higher scores.
However, we tried to mitigate this by including several various data sources in the benchmark and in the training data, mostly human-annotated. We encourage the deployment of tutoring models in any case with appropriate safeguards.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Scaffolding scores qualitative examples</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix A Scaffolding scores qualitative examples ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows assigned scores for various model and teacher responses given the problem and previous dialog. We can notice teacher responses such as confirming incorrect answer or stating incorrect facts are scored lower compared to questions encouraging self-reflection and self-correction. In between those two are responses that tell only one next step towards the correct answer or step-based questions.
Similarly, Table <a href="#A4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix D Details on Single-Criteria Classifiers ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> has examples of novice teacher responses from test set categorized into score quartiles. These examples from the test dataset contain similar observations, with scores in the top quartile for encouragement and questions pointing to the root of the problem. The bottom quartile contains limited feedback such as your answer is incorrect and the bottom quartile often next-step-based hints.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.18940v1/prompts2_3.svg" id="A1.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:471/542;" width="471" height="542"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Prompts for each task.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.T5" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A1.T5.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A1.T5.2.1" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="A1.T5.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Margaret wants to serve chicken salad sandwiches using mini croissants. Each committee member (24 people) will have 2 sandwiches. The bakery sells 12 mini croissants for $8.00. How much will she spend on croissants?</span>

<span id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Total sandwiches: <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="24\times 2=48" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>24</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">24\times 2=48</annotation></semantics></math></span>

</span></span>

<span id="A1.T5.2.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T5.2.7.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Student:</span> <span id="A1.T5.2.7.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">"I started by calculating how many sandwiches Margaret needs to make. Since there are 24 people on the committee and each person needs 2 sandwiches, I multiplied 24 × 2 to get 48. Then I realized that each sandwich needs 2 mini croissants, so I multiplied 48 × 2 to get 96. Since the bakery offers 12 mini croissants for $8.00, I divided 96 by 12 to get 8 sets of 12 mini croissants. Finally, I multiplied 8 × $8.00 to get my final answer of $64.00."</span></span>

Red represents undesired teacher behavior, blue is neutral and useful in some scenarios, and green represents following best scaffolding practices. Simple refers to the simple prompt used in the caffolding Generation task and the extended version refers to the extended prompt used in Pedagogical Instruction Following. </figcaption>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Task Prompts</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The exact prompts used in the benchmark are shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix A Scaffolding scores qualitative examples ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Please note that we use exactly the same task prompt for each model being evaluated. Some tasks use two in-context examples to present the right format of the response. The cost to run the full benchmark with GPT4o-mini is less than 3$. To run the open-weight models we use the vllm library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al. (2023)</a></cite>. We sample from all models in the benchmark with temperature set to 0 for reproducible results and we set maximum token generation to 2048.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Details of Benchmarked Models</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Specific versions of closed models we use are <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18</span> version and <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">learnlm-1.5-pro-experimental</span>. We use these exact versions of open-weight models loaded from Huggingface model hub <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wolf et al. (2020)</a></cite>: <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct</span>, <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct</span>, <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct</span>, <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CogBase-USTC/SocraticLM</span>, <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">princeton-nlp/Llemma-7B-32K-MathMix</span>, and <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Reward Model Details</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Training data</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training data used for training the Scaffolding reward model and its ablation are in Table <a href="#A0.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Implementation details</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We finetune all models using Huggingface transformers library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wolf et al. (2020)</a></cite> and
using the checkpoints from the Huggingface Model Hub respecting corresponding license agreements.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We finetune all models with a learning rate of <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\cdot 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\cdot 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> for 1 training epoch and with a batch size of 16. We use the AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We used an NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU and finetuning takes around 1 hour for each model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A3.F6.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="239.88" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 653.15 239.88" width="653.15"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,239.88) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 233.97 C 0 237.24 2.64 239.88 5.91 239.88 L 647.24 239.88 C 650.51 239.88 653.15 237.24 653.15 233.97 L 653.15 5.91 C 653.15 2.64 650.51 0 647.24 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 233.97 C 1.97 236.15 3.73 237.91 5.91 237.91 L 647.24 237.91 C 649.42 237.91 651.18 236.15 651.18 233.97 L 651.18 5.91 C 651.18 3.73 649.42 1.97 647.24 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 17.24)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:44.07em;--ltx-fo-height:15.09em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.25em;font-size:10pt;" height="212.32" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 208.86)" width="609.8"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

For LLM-as-a-judge, two utterances are listed the same way as in Figure <a href="#A3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ C.2 Implementation details ‣ Appendix C Reward Model Details ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Details on Single-Criteria Classifiers</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results of individual criteria classifiers on the separate test set are shown in Figure <a href="#A4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix D Details on Single-Criteria Classifiers ‣ MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-endedPedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. For training of the single-criteria classifiers we binarize the data from MRBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maurya et al. (2024)</a></cite>. In particular, we take the most negative criterion for each category as <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> and all others as <math id="A4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>.
We train <span id="A4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ModernBERT<math id="A4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math></span> with 149M parameters on NVIDIA V100 GPUs.
Again, we use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of <math id="A4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\cdot 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\cdot 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> and a batch size of 16 but train for 3 epochs due to the small data sizes. Training takes only ca. 15 minutes.</p>
</div>

</span></td></tr>
